turns.prompt_text: I have a bunch of these sparklers The metal seems to be like the stuff in paper clips I wonder if buying very cheap sparklers and bulk is a good way to get this kind of metal Or would it be more efficient just in a spool
turns.response_html:
You are spot on about the material—the core of a standard wire sparkler is almost always a low-carbon, mild steel wire, very similar to what is used to manufacture standard paper clips.

However, buying sparklers just to harvest the metal core is incredibly inefficient, both financially and practically. Buying a standalone spool of wire is a significantly better route for a few reasons:

1. The Cost per Foot is Way Higher with Sparklers

Even if you find dirt-cheap wholesale sparklers, you are paying for the chemical pyrotechnic composition (barium nitrate, iron/aluminum flakes, and binders), packaging, shipping restrictions, and manufacturing labor.

  • Sparklers: A bulk pack of 100 standard 10-inch sparklers might cost around $10 to $15. Once you strip away the pyrotechnic paste, you are left with 100 straight pieces of roughly 20-gauge wire, totaling about 83 feet of metal.
  • A Spool: You can walk into a hardware store or order online and get a 100-foot or even a 200-foot spool of galvanized or dark annealed steel wire (around 18 to 22 gauge) for $5 to $8.

2. The Harvest Labor is a Mess

The pyrotechnic coating on sparklers is designed to adhere tightly to the metal core so it doesn't flake off before use. Stripping it off manually while unburned is labor-intensive, incredibly messy, and leaves a lot of chemical residue on the metal. If you burn them first to get to the wire, the extreme heat oxidizes the steel, leaving it brittle, covered in a stubborn layer of black scale, and structurally weakened.

3. What to Look for in a Spool

If you like the structural properties of that sparkler core—decent stiffness but still easy to bend and form by hand—you want to look for these types of utility wire:

  • Galvanized Steel Wire (18 to 20 Gauge): This will give you the closest match to a high-quality paper clip. It has a zinc coating that keeps it shiny and prevents it from rusting.
  • Dark Annealed Wire / Mechanic's Wire: This is highly ductile (bends very easily without snapping) and is often used for tying or structuring. It has a darker, matte finish and is incredibly cheap.

Buying it on a spool gives you a continuous run of clean, unmarred, uniform metal without having to chip away chemical binders or clean up toxic dust.
